The gandharvas, adorned with gold, stood together with kings.
They wore golden-yellow upper garments and had variegated armor, chariots, and weapons.
Their crests rose toward the back of heaven, and their banners bore makaras of beryl.
The rākṣasas wore hibiscus-red upper garments and had red hair.
With vulture-banners, very powerful, they were adorned with spotless iron.
Holding pestles, swords, and maces, they were in chariots, wearing turbans and mail.
The nāgas roared like great clouds and carried dreadful meteors and thunderbolts as weapons.
The yakṣas wore black garments and held fearsome arrows and bows.
Fierce, with copper owl-banners, they were adorned with gold and jewels.
The night-roaming army shone with leopard-skin upper garments,
mostly with vulture-feathered standards and ornamented with ornaments of bone.
Armed with pestles, hard to behold, it resounded with the great cries of many creatures.
The kinnaras wore white garments and had white parasols and banners.
They mostly rode intoxicated elephants and had sharp lances as their weapons.
A swan, fashioned of silver and adorned with a net of pearls,
was the banner of the lord of the waters, with a terrible smoke-bannered fire.
But the upraised banner of <s>Dhanada</s> shone with branches of great ruby jewels,
as though it wished to go into the sky.
The great standard of <s>Yama</s> had a wolf made of wood and iron.
On the banner of the lord of rākṣasas appeared the face of a corpse-spirit.
The two gods <s>Candra</s> and <s>Arka</s>, of immeasurable splendor, had golden lion banners.
The banner of the two <s>Aśvins</s> had a jewel-spangled jar.
The banner of <s>Śatakratu</s> was made with a golden elephant, adorned with bright jewels,
and decorated with white yak-tail fans.
That army of the king of the gods, with nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, great serpents, and night-roamers,
was unconquerable in the three worlds.
There were thirty-three crores of hosts of the gods.
With white yak-tail fans like the Himalaya, with garlands beautiful like spotless golden lotuses,
with bright shoots of saffron glowing with deep red color, and crowded with rows of playful bees upon its cheeks,
there stood on the elephant named <s>Airāvata</s> the mighty <s>Pākaśāsana</s>, clothed in richly adorned garments.
He was adorned with a canopy of broad cloth and rays, and the tips of his arms were ringed with scattered armlets.
Praised by a thousand bards, the thousand-eyed one shone in heaven.
That army, filled with masses of horses and elephants and splendid with rows of white parasols and banners,
shone as an unconquerable force, crowded with winged arrows, hard to cross because of warriors bearing many weapons.
<s>Sūta</s> said:
In that extremely terrible collision of gods and asuras,
a very great tumult arose in both armies.
From the roaring of the gods and daityas and from the sound of conches and kettledrums,
and from the din of musical instruments and the trumpeting of elephants,
from the neighing of herds of horses and from the sound of chariot wheels,
and from the twanging of the bowstrings of heroes, an exceedingly great uproar arose.
When the two armies had met, each longing for victory over the other,
they were overwhelmed by anger and had set their minds on abandoning life.
Having met one another, they advanced in reverse order and with vigor:
a foot-soldier was engaged with a chariot, and a horseman with a chariot.
An elephant was joined with a foot-soldier, and in some place a chariot-warrior with another chariot-warrior.
Another elephant was joined with an elephant, and an elephant with many horses.
A single foot-soldier was matched with many maddened elephants.
Then, with lances, thunderbolts, maces, bhindipālas, and axes,
with spears, paṭṭiśas, tridents, clubs, kuṇapas, and gaḍas,
with discs and spikes, and with bright javelins and elephant-goads,
with karṇins, nālīkas, nārācas, vatsadantas, and half-moon arrows,
and with bhallas, śatapatras, and spotless parrot-beak arrows,
a shower of exceedingly wondrous form was seen in the sky.
Covering all the directions, it made everything as if filled with darkness.
They did not recognize one another in that dense darkness,
as, unseen, they hurled up a furious mass of missiles.
Fallen in the midst of the two armies, they looked at one another.
Then, with banners, arms, parasols, and heads with earrings,
with elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers, both falling and already fallen,
the earth was strewn like a sky-lake with lotuses fallen from it.
Elephants with broken tusks, split temples, and long great trunks cut off,
fell on the earth like mountains, streaming blood.
Chariots with their shafts, poles, wheels, and axles broken were shattered to pieces,
and horses by the thousands fell, reduced to fragments.
Then the earth became impassable with blood and flesh.
Rivers had eddies of blood and gave delight to flesh-eaters.
That crowded battlefield became a playground of vetālas.
<s>Sūta</s> said:
Then, seeing <s>Grasana</s>, <s>Yama</s>, dazed with anger,
rained down a shower of arrows, especially one blazing like fire.
Pierced by many arrows, the exceedingly valiant <s>Grasana</s>,
desiring to repay the deed done to him, bent his terrifying bow.
With five hundred extremely fierce arrows he struck <s>Yama</s>.
Considering <s>Grasana</s>'s arrows and his extraordinary manliness, <s>Yama</s>
assailed <s>Grasana</s> with fierce showers of arrows.
That shower of <s>Kṛtānta</s>'s arrows, spreading through the sky,
<s>Grasana</s>, lord of dānavas, cut apart with a shower of arrows.
Seeing that stream of arrows made fruitless, <s>Yama</s>

children.text: sa vicintya śaravrātaṃ grasanasya rathaṃ prati
children.translated_text: considered <s>Grasana</s>'s mass of arrows and aimed at his chariot.

children.text: cikṣepa mudgaraṃ ghoraṃ tarasā tasya cāntakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Then <s>Antaka</s> hurled a terrible club swiftly at him.

children.text: sa taṃ mudgaram āyāntam utplutya gaganasthitam
children.translated_text: Seeing that club coming, the son of the dānava leapt up into the sky,
and seized <s>Yama</s>'s weapon with his left hand.

children.text: tameva mudgaraṃ gṛhya yamasya mahiṣaṃ ruṣā
children.translated_text: Taking that very club, in anger he struck <s>Yama</s>'s buffalo,
and brought it down with force; it fell upon the ground.
Then <s>Yama</s>, springing up from that buffalo as it was about to fall,
struck <s>Grasana</s> hard in the face with a spear.
But from the blow of the spear he fell senseless to the ground.
Seeing <s>Grasana</s> fallen, <s>Jambha</s> of terrible valor
struck <s>Yama</s> in the chest with a bhindipāla.
From that blow, <s>Yama</s> streamed blood from his mouth.
Seeing <s>Kṛtānta</s> crushed, the mace-handed lord of wealth
advanced in anger against <s>Jambha</s>, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of yakṣas.
As he came on in anger, surrounded by the army of dānavas, <s>Jambha</s>

children.text: uvāca prājño vākyaṃ tu yathā snigdhena bhāṣitam ||
children.translated_text: spoke a prudent speech to him, as if it had been spoken with affection.
Then <s>Grasana</s>, having recovered consciousness, hurled his mace at <s>Yama</s>,
a heavy crusher of enemies, decorated with jewels and gold.
Seeing that inconceivable mace, the buffalo-mounted one
released, in order to counter the mace, his world-crushing and terrible
staff, surrounded by a wreath of flames, in anger.

children.text: sa gadāṃ viyati prāpya rarāsāmbudharo yathā ||
children.translated_text: It reached the mace in the sky and roared like a raincloud.
A collision arose between the two, unbearable as one between two mountains,
and the quarters were stunned by the crushing roar from those two.
The world became agitated, fearing the arrival of dissolution.
In a moment its roar grew quiet, though the sky was filled with blazing meteors,
as the terrible crushing of the two took place in the region of the heavens.
Then, after smashing the mace, the staff fell upon <s>Grasana</s>'s head,
firm and powerful, like misfortune stripping the prosperity from a man of bad conduct.

children.text: sa tu tena prahāreṇa dṛṣṭvā satimirā diśaḥ ||
children.translated_text: By that blow he saw the quarters covered with darkness,
and fell unconscious on the ground, adorned with the dust of the earth.
Then a dreadful cry of 'hā hā' arose in both armies.
Then, after only a muhūrta, <s>Grasana</s> regained consciousness
and saw his own body battered, with ornaments and garments disordered.
He then considered the act of making a counterstroke for what had been done:
'In the case of a man like me, when humiliation of one's lord has arisen,
the armies that depend on me are destroyed if I am defeated.
Let a man who acts as he pleases be of no account,
but not a man whose valued worth has been proclaimed hundreds of times in vain.'
Having reflected in this way, the mighty one sprang up swiftly.
Taking up a hammer like the staff of Time, mountain-like in form,
<s>Grasana</s>, of terrifying resolve, stood with his lips clenched together.
Hastening in his chariot, he approached <s>Antaka</s> in battle.

children.text: samāsādya yamaṃ yuddhe grasano bhrāmya mudgaram ||
children.translated_text: Having come up to <s>Yama</s> in the fight, <s>Grasana</s> whirled the hammer
and hurled the blazing, fearsome weapon with great speed at <s>Yama</s>'s head.
Seeing the blazing hammer, <s>Yama</s>'s eyes were shaken,
but the mighty one avoided the irresistible hammer.
When it had gone aside far away from him, that weapon of fierce and dreadful action

children.text: yāmyānāṃ kiṃkarāṇāṃ tu sahasraṃ niṣpipeṣa ha
children.translated_text: crushed a thousand of <s>Yama</s>'s kiṃkaras.
Then, seeing that terrible host of kiṃkaras slain,
he fell into supreme agitation, raising many kinds of weapons.
But <s>Grasana</s>, looking upon that army made up of kiṃkaras,
thought that thousands of <s>Yama</s>s had been created by <s>Yama</s>'s māyā.
Attacking the army, <s>Grasana</s> released showers of missiles,
and, resembling the horror at the end of a kalpa, became overwhelmed by anger.
Some he split with a spear, and some with straight-flying arrows;
some he crushed with a mace, and others with showers of hammers.
Some at that time were struck by terrible blows from prāsas,
while many others clung all around his arms.
Others struck him with stones, and others with very tall trees;
still others bit at his limbs even with their teeth.

children.text: apare muṣṭibhiḥ pṛṣṭhaṃ kiṃkarāḥ praharanti ca ||
children.translated_text: Other kiṃkaras struck his back with their fists.
Assailed in that way by the dreadful ones, <s>Grasana</s>, overwhelmed by anger,
threw bodies down on the surface of the earth and crushed them by the thousands.
Rising up, he struck some of the attacking kiṃkaras with his fists.
But through the battle with the kiṃkaras, <s>Grasana</s> became weary.

children.text: tamālokya yamaḥ śrāntaṃ nihatāṃ ca svavāhinīm
children.translated_text: Seeing him exhausted and his own army slain, <s>Yama</s>
came forward, raising his staff, mounted on his buffalo.
But as <s>Yama</s> approached, <s>Grasana</s> struck him in the chest with his mace.
Disregarding that deed of <s>Grasana</s>, <s>Antaka</s>, destroyer of foes,
angrily struck the foremost tigers of his chariot with his staff.
That chariot, its tigers crushed by the staff and half-broken, was dragged along,
like the mind of a man in doubt; such was the daitya's chariot.
Abandoning the chariot, the daitya went down onto the ground on foot.
Taking hold of <s>Yama</s> with both arms, the dānava fought him.
<s>Yama</s> too threw aside his weapons and engaged in hand-to-hand combat.
<s>Grasana</s>, swollen with strength, seized <s>Yama</s> by the waist-cloths
and whirled him swiftly, as agitation whirls the mind.
<s>Yama</s> too braced the daitya at the neck with his pair of arms,
lifted him up from the surface of the earth, and whirled him with force.
Then the two, merciless, struck each other with their fists.
Because of the daitya lord's immense size, <s>Yama</s>'s arms then grew tired,
and, placing his face on the daitya's shoulder, he sought rest.
Then the daitya, perceiving <s>Antaka</s> to be exhausted, with force
crushed him many times on the surface of the earth with heels and hands,
until much blood flowed from <s>Yama</s>'s face.

children.text: nirjīvitaṃ yamaṃ dṛṣṭvā tataḥ saṃtyajya dānavaḥ
children.translated_text: Then, seeing <s>Yama</s> bereft of life, the dānava let him go,

children.text: jayaṃ prāpyoddhataṃ daityo nādaṃ muktvā mahāsvanaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and the arrogant daitya, having won victory, let out a great loud roar.
He himself reached his army and stood immovable like a mountain,
while <s>Jambha</s>, with arrows that pierced vital points, attacked the lord of wealth.
The quarters were blocked by the enraged one, and his army was cut to pieces.
Then the lord of wealth, overcome by anger, attacked the dānava <s>Jambha</s>.
He pierced him in the heart with a thousand arrows bright as fire,

children.text: sārathiṃ ca śatenājau dhvajaṃ daśabhireva ca ||
children.translated_text: and in the battle he pierced his charioteer with a hundred arrows and his banner with ten.
He struck his two hands with seventy-five shafts, and his bow with ten,
with peacock-feathered, oil-polished, straight-flying arrows.
With one arrow he pierced the lion, and with ten sharp arrows he pierced him.
But <s>Jambha</s>, seeing that very difficult deed of the lord of wealth,
took courage in his heart, though his mind was somewhat frightened.
He seized sharp arrows that could pierce the vital points of an enemy.
With his bow drawn back to his ear, <s>Jambha</s>, flooded with anger,
the dānava pierced <s>Dhanada</s> in the chest with sharp arrows.
And with a firm arrow he struck his charioteer in the heart.
Then with one oil-polished arrow the dānava cut his bowstring.
Then, with sharp, dreadful arrows that pierced vital points,
the cruel doer pierced <s>Vitteśa</s> in the breast with ten arrows.
The lord of wealth, firmly pierced, went into a deep swoon.
But after a moment he took courage and drew his terrible bow.
Scattering thousands of sharp arrows, the lord of wealth
filled the quarters, the sky, the intermediate directions, the earth, and the asura's armies
with speed, covering the disk of the sun.
<s>Jambha</s> too, in the great battle, with many arrows
cut them down one by one, setting his shafts swiftly, by his extraordinary valor.
Then <s>Dhaneśa</s>, enraged by the deed of the lord of dānavas,
shattered his armies with showers of many kinds of arrows.
Seeing that destructive deed of the superintendent of wealth, the dānava
took up a terrible iron club adorned with gold.
He crushed by the thousands the yakṣas who attended <s>Dhanada</s>.
As they were being slain by the daitya, they uttered terrible cries.
They all surrounded the chariot of the lord of wealth and took their stand.
Seeing them afflicted, the god grasped a dreadful spear.
With it he quickly slew thousands of daityas.
As the daityas were being destroyed, the dānava, dazed with anger,
the daitya seized an axe, a crusher of the enemies of the daityas.
With that sharp-edged weapon the daitya attacked the great chariot of the lord of wealth.
The daitya cut it into hundreds of pieces, as a mouse cuts soft cloth.
Then <s>Vitteśa</s>, on foot, took up a terrifying mace,
one that destroys proud enemies amid the crush of great battles,
unassailable by all beings and worshipped for many years,
its body smeared with various sandal pastes and scented with divine flowers,
pure, made of iron, heavy, unerring, and adorned with gold.

children.text: cikṣepa mūrdhni saṃkruddho jambhasya tu dhanādhipaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Enraged, the lord of wealth hurled it at <s>Jambha</s>'s head.
Seeing it coming, adorned like a mass of lightning flashes,
the daitya released a shower of weapons to strike the mace.
He sent disks, kuṇapas, lances, bhuśuṇḍīs, and paṭṭiśas
with his two arms bound by golden armlets, fierce in valor.
But it made all those weapons useless and, on the daitya's chest,
fell flashing and fierce, like a great meteor in a mountain cave.
Struck hard by it, he fell onto the chariot box.
Streams of blood flowed from him as he lost consciousness.

children.text: jambhaṃ tu nihataṃ matvā kujambho bhairavasvanaḥ
children.translated_text: But thinking <s>Jambha</s> slain, <s>Kujambha</s> of terrifying voice
became enraged against the lord of wealth and was filled with extreme fury.

children.text: cakre bāṇamayaṃ jālaṃ dikṣu yakṣādhipasya tu
children.translated_text: He made a net of arrows in the quarters around the lord of yakṣas.
Then he cut that net of arrows with sharp crescent-headed shafts.

children.text: mumoca śaravṛṣṭiṃ tu tasmai yakṣādhipo balī
children.translated_text: The mighty lord of yakṣas released a shower of arrows at him.

children.text: sa taṃ daityaḥ śaravrātaṃ cicheda niśitaiḥ śaraiḥ ||
children.translated_text: That daitya cut that mass of arrows with sharp arrows.

children.text: vyarthīkṛtāṃ tu tāṃ dṛṣṭvā śaravṛṣṭiṃ dhanādhipaḥ
children.translated_text: Seeing that shower of arrows made useless, the lord of wealth
grasped an irresistible spear, laughing with golden bells.
With an arm that shone with the radiance of jeweled armlets,

children.text: sa tāṃ nirūpya vegena kujambhāya mumoca ha ||
children.translated_text: he aimed it and swiftly released it at <s>Kujambha</s>.
It tore open <s>Kujambha</s>'s dreadful heart,
like a cultivated desire for wealth in a man of little strength.
Then, after splitting his heart, it went down to the surface of the earth.
After a moment the dānava of dreadful form, unsteady,
the daitya seized a tall paṭṭiśa with a sharp stone-like point.
With that paṭṭiśa, in battle, he pierced the space between <s>Dhanada</s>'s breasts,
like a harshly formed speech creeping into the inner vital places,
as a wicked man pierces the heart of one well-born.
By that blow of the paṭṭiśa, <s>Dhaneśa</s> fainted.
He fell onto the seat of the chariot, like a worn-out bearer of a yoke.

children.text: tathāgataṃ tu taṃ dṛṣṭvā dhaneśaṃ naravāhanam
children.translated_text: Seeing the man-mounted <s>Dhaneśa</s> brought to such a state,
the god <s>Nirṛti</s>, armed with a sword and followed by forces of night-roamers,
rushed swiftly at <s>Kujambha</s> of terrible valor.

children.text: atha dṛṣṭvā tu durdharṣaṃ kujambho rākṣaseśvaram ||
children.translated_text: Then, seeing the irresistible lord of rākṣasas, <s>Kujambha</s>
urged his armies on toward the slaying of the lord of rākṣasas.
Seeing the army driven on, terrifying with bhalla arrows and many weapons,
he leapt swiftly from his chariot, shining with the radiance of his ornaments.
With his unsheathed sword, gleaming like the sky, as if cutting lotuses,
he cut off the varied faces of his enemies on every side.
Sideways, behind him, below, and above, the long-armed hero with his great sword
with lips clenched between his teeth, a fierce grimace, and a contracted brow,
his eyes reddened by violent anger, cut down the dānavas in battle.
Then, seeing his own army almost entirely destroyed,
<s>Kujambha</s>, leaving <s>Dhanada</s>, rushed against the lord of rākṣasas.
Then <s>Jambha</s>, having regained consciousness, seized the attendants of the lord of wealth
alive as prisoners, binding them by the thousands with nooses.

children.text: mūrtimanti tu ratnāni vividhāni ca dānavāḥ
children.translated_text: The dānavas also took the various embodied jewels,
the divine vehicles, and aerial cars by the thousands.
Then the lord of wealth, having regained consciousness, saw that condition,
and, breathing long and hot in anger, his eyes copper-red,

children.text: dhyātvāstraṃ gāruḍaṃ divyaṃ bāṇaṃ saṃdhāya kārmuke
children.translated_text: meditated on the divine Garuḍa missile, set an arrow on his bow,
and released that enemy-tearing arrow into the army of the dānavas.
First, streams of smoke issued from his bow;
after that came millions of sparks of blazing brilliance.
Then the missile made the sky filled with flames on every side;
then, step by step, it became irresistible and manifold in form.
The world became as though formless, covered over with darkness.
Then in the mid-air they proclaimed that purified brilliance.
<s>Kujambha</s>, that dānava of exceeding valor, observed it
and, roaring, rushed swiftly on foot toward <s>Dhanada</s>.
Then, seeing the daitya coming face to face, the lord of wealth
was seized with alarm and intent on flight.
Then, as he fled, his jewel-adorned crown
fell blazing to the ground like the disk of the sun from the sky.
For noble heroes, when their lord has withdrawn from battle,
it is fitting to die at the head of the combat, before that ornament.
Having so resolved, the unassailable yakṣas, holding many weapons and missiles,

children.text: yuyutsavaḥ sthitā yakṣā mukuṭaṃ parivārya tam ||
children.translated_text: stood eager to fight, surrounding that crown.
Those brave followers of <s>Dhanada</s>, rich in pride,
the dānava of fierce manliness saw with indignation.
Taking up a terrifying bhuśuṇḍī club, heavy as a mountain,
he crushed the night-roamers who were guarding the crown.
Having crushed them, the danuja then placed that crown
on his own chariot; the foe of the immortals had defeated <s>Dhanada</s> in battle.

children.text: dhanāni ratnāni ca mūrtimanti tathā nidhānāni śarīriṇaśca
children.translated_text: The wealth, the embodied jewels, and likewise the treasures with bodies,

children.text: ādāya sarvāṇi jagāma daityo jambhaḥ svasainyaṃ danujendrasiṃhaḥ
children.translated_text: all these the daitya <s>Jambha</s>, lion among danuja lords, took and went to his own army.

children.text: dhanādhipo vai vinikīrṇamūrdhajo jagāma dīnaḥ surabharturantikam ||
children.translated_text: The lord of wealth, his hair disheveled, went miserably to the lord of the gods.
Then the delight of the night-roamers, locked in combat with <s>Kujambha</s>,
resorted to an unfailing dark illusion, the lord of rākṣasas.
He bewildered the daitya lord, making the world full of darkness.
Then the forces of the dānavas, their eyes rendered useless,

children.text: na śekuścalitaṃ tatra padādapi padaṃ tadā
children.translated_text: could not move there even a single step from where they stood.
Then, with a shower of many missiles, he struck the great army of the dānavas,
whose mounts were distressed by dense mist and darkness.
While the daityas were being slain and <s>Kujambha</s> was bewildered in mind,
<s>Mahiṣa</s>, lord of the dānavas, resembling a cloud at the end of an age,
fashioned the Sāvitra missile, adorned with masses of meteors.
When the supreme, blazing Sāvitra missile expanded,
the terrible and intense darkness immediately came to destruction.
Then the missile, marked with flashing sparks, destroyed all the darkness,
like a clear autumn lake filled with masses of blossoming red lotuses.
Then, when the darkness had subsided, the daitya lords regained their sight
and, with cruel minds, began a wondrous battle with the armies of the gods.
By weapons released in anger, the serpent missile was driven away.
Then, taking up a terrible bow and arrows like venomous snakes,
<s>Kujambha</s> rushed swiftly toward the army of the rākṣasa king.
The lord of rākṣasas, with his attendants, saw him coming
and pierced him with sharp arrows, fearsome like cruel venomous snakes.

children.text: tadādānaṃ ca saṃdhānaṃ na mokṣaścāpi lakṣyate ||
children.translated_text: His taking up of the arrows, his setting them on the bow, and even his release of them could not be seen.
With his own arrows, by extreme swiftness, he cut apart the volleys of his arrows.
With an exceedingly sharp arrow he cut down the banner, bright with workmanship, of the foe of the immortals,
and with a bhalla arrow he knocked his charioteer down from the chariot-seat.
<s>Kujambha</s>, seeing that deed of the lord of rākṣasas in battle,
his eyes red with anger, leapt from his chariot, the dānava,
and swiftly seized a sword clear as the autumn sky,
and a shield adorned with ten crescent-moon ornaments.
The daitya charged the lord of rākṣasas in battle with force.
When he had come near, the lord of rākṣasas struck him in the chest with a club.

children.text: sa tu tena prahāreṇa kṣīṇaḥ saṃbhrāntamānasaḥ ||
children.translated_text: By that blow he was weakened, his mind thrown into confusion,
and the danuja stood motionless, like a steadfast mountain.
After a moment the unconquerable lord of dānavas recovered himself,
mounted his chariot, and seized the rākṣasa with his left hand.
The daitya, having seized <s>Nirṛti</s> by the hair and pinned him down with his knee,
then, in fury, wished to cut off his head with his sword.
At that very moment the god <s>Varuṇa</s>, lord of the waters, quickly
bound the two arms of the lord of dānavas with his noose.
Then the noose-bearer struck with his mace the daitya whose arms were bound
and whose manly power had been made useless, abandoning pity.

children.text: sa tu tena prahāreṇa srotobhiḥ kṣatajaṃ vaman ||
children.translated_text: By that blow, vomiting blood in streams,
he assumed the form of a cloud wreathed with vine-like garlands of lightning.
Seeing <s>Kujambha</s> brought to that condition, <s>Mahīṣāsura</s>,
with a gaping, deep mouth, wished to swallow both gods,
<s>Nirṛti</s> and <s>Varuṇa</s>, his face fierce with sharp fangs.
The two, recognizing the evil intention of that daitya,
left the chariot path in terror because of <s>Mahīṣa</s>'s excessive speed;

children.text: bhṛśaṃ drutau javād digbhyām ubhābhyāṃ bhayavihvalau
children.translated_text: both fled very swiftly in different directions, overwhelmed with fear.
<s>Nirṛti</s> quickly went for refuge to <s>Pākaśāsana</s>.
But the enraged daitya <s>Mahīṣa</s> rushed upon <s>Varuṇa</s>.
Seeing him intent on the mouth of death, the moon, radiant like the Himalaya,
made an icy mass of thorn-like hail issuing from the soma-weapon,
and <s>Candra</s> made a second, matchless wind-weapon.

children.text: vāyunā tena candreṇa saṃśuṣkeṇa himena ca
children.translated_text: By that wind, by <s>Candra</s>, and by the drying frost,
all the dānavas were afflicted, cut down by cold and bereft of valor.
They could neither move with their feet nor even take up weapons.
By the great fall of snow and by weapons impelled by the moon,
the bodies of the asura army were burned on every side.
<s>Mahīṣa</s>, powerless, his face trembling with cold,
sat down facing downward, holding his armpits with his hands.
All those daityas, unable to make any countermeasure and conquered by the moon,
abandoned from afar their desire for battle and stood there seeking to live.
There <s>Kālanemi</s>, blazing with anger, spoke to the daityas:

children.text: bho bhoḥ śṛṅgāriṇaḥ śarāḥ sarve śastrāstrapāragāḥ
children.translated_text: Ho! ho! O horned heroes, all of you skilled in weapons and missiles,
each one of you is able to balance the whole world with his arms;
each one of you is able to swallow the whole moving and unmoving world;
even all the gods are not sufficient for any one of you,
mighty as you are, to equal even a sixteenth part, with all effort.
Why, defeated by the immortals, have you gone off and now stand still in battle?
This is not fitting for heroes, especially for those born among daityas.
And our king <s>Tāraka</s>, destroyer of worlds, is away;
angered at your withdrawal from this battle, he will take your lives.
With their hearing destroyed by cold and their skill in speech likewise gone,
the daityas then became mute, their rows of teeth chattering.
Seeing those daityas senseless and overcome by cold,
the great asura <s>Kālanemi</s>, thinking the action suited to the time,

children.text: āśritya dānavīṃ māyāṃ vitatya svaṃ mahāvapuḥ ||
children.translated_text: resorted to dānava magic and expanded his own great body;

children.text: pūrayāmāsa gaganaṃ diśo vidiśa eva ca
children.translated_text: he filled the sky and the directions and intermediate directions.
The lord of dānavas fashioned ten thousand suns in his body,
and by magic he filled the quarters with fierce fires.
Then in a moment the whole triple world became filled with flames.
By that mass of flames, the moon lost its power.
Then, step by step, the cold gloomy weather was dispelled.
That force of the lords of dānavas was restored through <s>Kālanemi</s>'s magic.
Seeing that dānava army restored to consciousness, <s>Divākara</s>,
agitated, the single eye of the world, spoke to <s>Aruṇa</s> in anger:
<s>Divākara</s> said:
Drive the chariot quickly, <s>Aruṇa</s>, to where <s>Kālanemi</s>'s chariot is.
There a fierce collision will occur, a destruction of heroes.
Here <s>Śaśāṅka</s>, whose strength we relied upon, has been defeated.
Thus addressed, the elder brother of <s>Garuḍa</s> drove the chariot,
with the horses carefully controlled, adorned with garlands of white chowries.
Then the blessed lamp of the world grasped his outstretched bow
and two arrows, noble and divine, shining like venomous serpents.
Aiming one arrow with the <s>saṃcāra</s> weapon of transference, he released it,
and he let fly the second, joined with an illusion.
With the <s>saṃcāra</s> weapon he instantly made an exchange of forms:

children.text: devānāṃ dānavaṃ rūpaṃ dānavānāṃ ca daivikam
children.translated_text: the gods had dānava form, and the dānavas had divine form.
Mistaking his own followers for gods, he struck them with the agility of his terrible weapons;
<s>Kālanemi</s>, filled with rage, was like Death at the end of an age.
Some he struck with a sharp sword, some with showers of iron arrows,
some with dreadful maces, and some with terrible axes.
With fierce speed he cut off the heads of some, and the arms, chariots, and charioteers of others;
then he crushed some by the speed of his chariot, and others in anger with blows of his raised fist.
When <s>Nemi</s>, lord of dānavas, saw his own men slain in battle,

children.text: rūpaṃ svaṃ tu prapadyanta hyasurāḥ suradharṣitāḥ ||
children.translated_text: the asuras, harassed by the gods, were returning to their own form.
But <s>Kālanemi</s>, filled with rage, did not recognize their form.
Then the daitya <s>Nemi</s>, seeing them, said to <s>Kālanemi</s>:

children.text: ahaṃ nemiḥ suro naiva kālaneme vidasva mām
children.translated_text: I am <s>Nemi</s>, not a god; know me, <s>Kālanemi</s>.
Deluded by you in battle, many mighty warriors have been slain,
ten lakhs of daityas here, unconquerable by the gods.
Release at once the <s>Brahmāstra</s>, the weapon that wards off all weapons.
Awakened by that, the daitya, his mind agitated with alarm,
fitted an arrow that had been empowered with the <s>Brahmāstra</s>.

children.text: mumoca cāpi daityendraḥ sa svayaṃ surakaṇṭakaḥ
children.translated_text: And the lord of daityas himself, the tormentor of the gods, released it.
Then the three worlds, with all that moves and does not move, were pervaded by the weapon's splendor.
The entire army of the gods became filled with fear.
And the Saṃcara weapon, pacified, shone of itself on the battlefield.
When that weapon had been checked, the sun, his brilliance diminished,
resorted to <s>Mahendra</s>'s magic and multiplied his own body by crores.
With the descent of his blazing rays he overwhelmed the three worlds,
and scorched the army of dānavas, whose streams of marrow and blood ran out.
Then from every side he rained down fire, packed together densely.
The lord made the eyes of the dānava chiefs blind.
The rut-fluid of the elephants melted away, and they fell upon the ground with cries.
The horses breathed hard, and the chariot-warriors too were afflicted by heat.
Here and there, tortured by thirst, they sought water,
and also shaded branches and the caverns of mountains.
As they sought coolness, creeping among the trees,
a forest fire blazed up, with terrible flames and trees burned away.
Seeing water before them, wreathed with waves, while they longed for drink,
they could not reach it, though it stood before them, because they were crushed down.
Failing to obtain water, they lay on the ground, mouths gaping and consciousness gone.

children.text: tatra tatra vyadṛśyanta mṛtā daityeśvarā bhuvi
children.translated_text: There, here and there, dead lords of daityas were seen upon the earth.
Chariots and elephants had fallen, and horses too had perished.
Standing, vomiting, and running, with blood, fat, and gore streaming down,
thousands of dānavas were seen lying dead.
When that great destruction of the dānava chiefs was taking place,
<s>Kālanemi</s>, his eyes copper-red from rising fury and tormented by wrath,
became like a cloud of the end of an age, flashing with many hundreds of lightning bolts,
and with deep thunderclaps he struck at the heart of the world.
Covering the expanse of the sky, he destroyed the sun's illusion.
He rained cool water upon the army of the dānava chiefs.
Having obtained that rain, the daityas then gradually revived,
unwithered, like sprouts from seed when they receive rain upon the earth.
Then that great asura <s>Kālanemi</s>, having taken the form of a cloud,
rained a fierce, unconquerable shower of weapons upon the armies of the gods.
Harassed by that shower from the mighty lords of daityas,

children.text: gatiṃ kāṃ ca na paśyanto gāvaḥ śītārditā iva ||
children.translated_text: and seeing no course at all, they were like cows afflicted by cold.
They pressed against one another's backs, their hands letting their weapons fall.

children.text: sveṣu bādhe vyalīyanta gajeṣu turageṣu ca ||
children.translated_text: Under their own distress they hid among their elephants and horses.
The immortals, terrified by weapons, concealed themselves here and there among the chariots.
Others, their limbs drawn in and their faces covered with their own hands,
wandered about bewildered, this way and that, through the ten directions.
In such a tumultuous battle, while the gods were being destroyed,
there were seen on the ground those whose joints of limb had been split by weapons,
with arms torn off, heads broken, and thighs and knees cut away,
with chariot assemblies overturned and rows of banners crushed,
with horses whose bodies were pierced and elephants resembling mountains,
and with pools of flowing blood the earth appeared horribly transformed.
Thus in the battle the powerful daitya, the great asura <s>Kālanemi</s>,
in a single moment slew ten ayutas of gandharvas,
five lakhs of yakṣas and six ayutas of rākṣasas.

children.text: trīṇi lakṣāṇi jaghne sa kiṃnarāṇāṃ tarasvinām
children.translated_text: He slew three lakhs of swift kinnaras,
and, fearless, seven lakhs of the chief piśācas.
Of the other hosts belonging to the races of gods, countless numbers
he angrily slew by crores, skilled in weapons and using varied missiles.
When the immortals were being destroyed in that dreadful humiliation,
the two gods, the <s>Aśvins</s>, grew enraged, shining with wondrous weapons and armor.
In battle they struck the daitya, who was like the fire of death.
Encountering that terrible one in battle, each of them, with sixty arrows,
struck the dreadful-looking asura in his vital points with sharp-tipped shafts.
Under the blows of their arrows, his mind was somewhat distressed.
He seized an eight-spoked discus, washed with oil and ending battles.
With that discus he cut the yoke-poles of the <s>Aśvins</s>' chariots.
Then the daitya took up a bow and arrows like venomous serpents.
He rained them upon the heads of the physicians, covering the course of the sky.
But the two of them cut those daitya arrows apart with sharp weapons.
Seeing that deed of theirs, he was astonished and entered into anger.
With great rage he took up an all-iron crusher,
a terrible club, fearsome as the rod of death.

children.text: sa tato bhrāmya vegena cikṣepāśvirathaṃ prati
children.translated_text: Then, whirling it with speed, he hurled it toward the <s>Aśvins</s>' chariot.
Seeing that club coming through the sky,

children.text: tyaktvā rathau tu tau vegādāplutau tarasāśvinau
children.translated_text: the two <s>Aśvins</s> swiftly abandoned their chariots and leapt away with speed.

children.text: tau rathau sa tu niṣpiṣya mudgaro'calasaṃnibhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: That mountain-like club crushed those two chariots,
and, adorned with a golden net, tore open the earth.
Seeing his deed, the two <s>Aśvins</s>, the physicians skilled in wondrous combat,
then prepared the thunderbolt weapon to check the lord of dānavas.
Then a rain made of vajras began, exceedingly terrible.
By the dreadful blows of vajras that lord of daityas was assailed.

children.text: ratho dhvajo dhanuścakraṃ kavacaṃ cāpi kāñcanam ||
children.translated_text: His chariot, banner, bow, wheel, and golden armor too
in a moment were reduced to bits like sesame seeds, while the whole army watched.
Seeing that difficult deed, he of fearsome valor, against the two <s>Aśvins</s>,
the mighty one released the <s>Nārāyaṇa</s>-astra at the head of the battle.
The lord of dānavas quieted the vajra-astra by the fiery power of his own missile.
When that vajra-astra had been calmed, <s>Kālanemi</s> immediately
set about trying to seize the two <s>Aśvins</s> alive.
Those two <s>Aśvins</s>, frightened from the battle, went toward the chariot of the thousand-eyed one,
trembling, on foot, and deprived of weapons.
The daitya <s>Kālanemi</s>, very mighty, followed those two,
and the cruel one reached <s>Indra</s>'s chariot, attended by the ranks of the daityas.
Seeing him, all beings became terrified and bewildered.
Seeing that cruelty of the daitya, all beings thought
that <s>Mahendra</s>'s defeat would bring about the destruction of all worlds.
The chief mountains shook; meteors fell from the sky.
Clouds thundered in the quarters, and the great oceans rose up.
Seeing that disturbance among beings, the blessed one whose banner is <s>Garuḍa</s>
awoke on his serpent couch, abandoning his yogic sleep.
The lotuses of his feet were constantly caressed by the two hands of <s>Lakṣmī</s>.
The lord's bodily radiance was like a blue lotus in an autumn sky.
His chest shone with the <s>Kaustubha</s>, and he was brilliant with beautiful armlets.
Reflecting on the distress of the gods, he summoned <s>Vainateya</s>.
When he had been summoned and stood there, while the lord's body had been resting on the serpent,
he mounted him, blazing with the sharp flames of many divine weapons, and himself went to the gods.
There he saw <s>Devendra</s> attacked and overwhelmed
by lords of dānavas, dark as new rain clouds and fierce in manliness,
just as a man of noble lineage may be beset by dreadful misfortunes,
while a pure deed, done in a worthy field, quickly comes for his protection.
Then the daiteyas saw in the sky a disk of light
flashing like the sun, with hot rays, standing on the mountain of sunrise.
Wishing to know the power of that brilliance,
the dānavas saw <s>Garutmant</s>, resembling the fire at the end of an age.
And they saw imperishable <s>Acyuta</s> seated upon him, with the radiance of a mass of clouds.
Looking upon him, the lords of asuras were filled with joy in their minds.
"This indeed is the whole treasure of the gods; if he is conquered, the gods are conquered.
This <s>Keśava</s>, the slayer of foes, is death itself for the circles of daityas.
Relying on him, the immortals enjoy the shares of sacrifice in the worlds."
Having said this, all the dānavas surrounded him on every side,
and with various astras they struck him as he came into the battle.
Ten great-chariot daityas, beginning with <s>Kālanemi</s>,
<s>Kālanemi</s> pierced <s>Janārdana</s> with sixty arrows.
<s>Nimi</s> pierced him with a hundred arrows, and <s>Mathana</s> with eighty shafts.
<s>Jambhaka</s> pierced him with seventy, and <s>Śumbha</s> with only ten.
All the remaining daitya lords, each in turn, struck <s>Viṣṇu</s> with arrows,
and, intent on the fight, they struck him together with <s>Garuḍa</s>, ten arrows each, in battle.
Not enduring that deed of theirs, <s>Viṣṇu</s>, the slayer of dānavas,
struck each dānava with six straight-flying arrows apiece.
Then <s>Kālanemi</s>, with three arrows drawn back to the ear,
pierced <s>Viṣṇu</s> in the heart, his eyes red from anger.
Those heated-gold arrows shone in his heart
like bright rays of the <s>Kaustubha</s>, blazing clearly.
Somewhat distressed by those arrows, <s>Hari</s> seized a mudgara club.
Whirling it continually with force, he hurled it at the dānava.
Before it reached him, the lord of dānavas, while it was still in the sky, with hundreds of arrows
angrily cut it into bits like sesame seeds, displaying the lightness of his hand.

children.text: tato viṣṇuḥ prakupitaḥ prāsaṃ jagrāha bhairavam
children.translated_text: Then <s>Viṣṇu</s>, enraged, seized a terrifying lance.
With it he struck the daitya hard in the heart.
After a moment the great asura <s>Kālanemi</s> regained consciousness
and seized a sharp-pointed śakti, clanging loudly with golden bells.
With it the son of <s>Diti</s> pierced <s>Viṣṇu</s>'s left arm.
His arm, split by the śakti and streaming blood, shone
as though adorned with an armlet made of ruby.

children.text: tato viṣṇuḥ prakupito jagrāha vipulaṃ dhanuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Then <s>Viṣṇu</s>, enraged, seized a great bow
and seventeen sharp nārāca arrows, piercers of vital spots.

children.text: daityasya hṛdayaṃ ṣaḍbhirvivyādha ca tribhiḥ śaraiḥ ||
children.translated_text: With six he pierced the daitya's heart, and with three arrows struck him again.

children.text: caturbhiḥ sārathiṃ cāsya dhvajaṃ caikena pattriṇā
children.translated_text: With four he pierced his charioteer, and with one feathered shaft his banner.

children.text: dvābhyāṃ jyādhanuṣī cāpi bhujaṃ savyaṃ ca pattriṇā ||
children.translated_text: With two he pierced both bowstring and bow, and with one feathered shaft his left arm.

children.text: sa viddho hṛdaye gāḍhaṃ daityo hariśilīmukhaiḥ
children.translated_text: The daitya, deeply pierced in the heart by <s>Hari</s>'s arrows,
was tall and reddened by flowing blood, his mind overcome by pain.
He trembled like a kiṃśuka tree driven by the wind.
Seeing him trembling, <s>Keśava</s> seized a mace.

children.text: tāṃ ca vegena cikṣepa kālanemirathaṃ prati
children.translated_text: He hurled it swiftly toward <s>Kālanemi</s>'s chariot.
That fierce, massive mace fell upon <s>Kālanemi</s>'s head.
The asura's head was crushed, and his crown was smashed.
With torrents of blood flowing from his openings, he was like a mountain with its ores running.
When his chariot had broken, he fell unconscious, with only his life remaining;
and to the dānava fallen in the chariot-seat, <s>Acyuta</s>, slayer of foes,
the lord whose weapon is the discus, first smiled and spoke this statement:
"Go, asura. You are released for the present; live without fear.
After a short time I myself will be your end."
Hearing that speech of his, the charioteer of <s>Kālanemi</s>
drove the chariot away and brought <s>Kālanemi</s> far off.
<s>Sūta</s> said:

children.text: taṃ dṛṣṭvā dānavāḥ kruddhāśceruḥ svaiḥ svairbalairvṛtāḥ
children.translated_text: Seeing him, the dānavas, enraged, moved about, surrounded by their own respective forces,
in every direction, like bees when honey is being carried off.
On an elephant adorned with a net of black yak-tail fans and with auspicious ornamented projections,
bearing five variegated banners and with its temples split open,
a dreadful elephant, mountain-like, streaming rut, hard to restrain,
the mighty daitya <s>Nimi</s> mounted in battle and advanced against <s>Hari</s>.
With him were fierce dānavas, foot-guards of the elephant,
twenty-seven thousand, shining with crowns and armor.
<s>Mathana</s> was mounted on a horse, and <s>Jambhaka</s> had a camel as his vehicle;
<s>Śumbha</s> too mounted a huge ram and went toward the battle.
Other lords of the dānavas, intent and holding many kinds of weapons,
angrily struck in battle <s>Viṣṇu</s>, whose action is unwearied.
The daitya <s>Nimi</s> struck with an iron club, and <s>Mathana</s> with a hammer;
<s>Śumbha</s> with a sharp spear, and <s>Grasana</s> likewise with a lance;

children.text: cakreṇa mahiṣaḥ kruddho jambhaḥ śaktyā mahāraṇe
children.translated_text: the enraged <s>Mahiṣa</s> with a discus, and <s>Jambha</s> with a śakti in the great battle;
all struck <s>Nārāyaṇa</s>, while the rest struck him with sharp arrows.
Those weapons, once hurled, entered <s>Hari</s>'s body
like instructions spoken by a teacher and taught into the ear of a good pupil.
Unshaken in battle, <s>Viṣṇu</s> then took up his bow
and arrows shaped like venomous serpents, oil-polished and straight.
Then, taking aim at those daityas, with his bow drawn back to the ear,
he rushed angrily in battle against the army of daityas, by his prowess.
He pierced <s>Nimi</s> with twenty arrows blazing like fire,
<s>Mathana</s> with ten arrows, and <s>Śumbha</s> with only five.
Angrily he pierced <s>Mahiṣa</s> in the chest with a single feathered arrow,
<s>Jambha</s> with twelve sharp ones, and all the others one by one with eight each.
Seeing that agility of his, the dānavas were overcome with anger;
roaring, they made a most wondrous battle with effort.
Then the dānava <s>Nimi</s> cut <s>Viṣṇu</s>'s bow with a bhalla arrow;
and <s>Mahiṣāsura</s> cut the arrow being set in his hand.
<s>Jambha</s> tormented <s>Garuḍa</s> with sharp shafts,
and <s>Śumbha</s>, mountain-like, struck his arm hard.

children.text: chinne dhanuṣi govindo gadāṃ jagrāha bhīṣaṇām
children.translated_text: When his bow was cut, <s>Govinda</s> took up a terrifying mace
and sent it with force at <s>Mathana</s> in the great battle.
Before it reached him, <s>Nimi</s> cut it to sesame-sized pieces with arrows in the fight;
and he saw it come to destruction, like a request whose object has been lost.
He took up a dreadful hammer adorned with divine jewels
and then released it swiftly, aiming at the dānava <s>Nimi</s>.

children.text: tam āyāntaṃ viyatyeva trayo daityā nyavārayan
children.translated_text: As it was coming through the sky, three daityas checked it there itself:
the daitya <s>Jambha</s> with a mace, and <s>Grasana</s> with a paṭṭiśa;
and the daitya <s>Mahiṣa</s> with a śakti, desiring victory for his own side.
Seeing it repelled, like affection directed toward a wicked man,
he took up a śakti with a fierce point, making the harsh sound of eight bells,
and, aiming it at <s>Jambha</s>, he hurled it, terrible in battle.
The elephant, delight of the dānavas, seized it while it was in the sky;
and he saw it seized, like instruction grasped by discerning people.
Taking another bow, firm, able to bear weight, and strong in substance,
he aimed the Raudra missile and released an arrow against him.
Then by the brilliance of that missile the whole world, moving and unmoving, was pervaded;
then everything in the sky appeared to be made of arrows.
The earth, the directions, and the intermediate directions became filled with a net of arrows.
Seeing the greatness of that missile, the asura general <s>Grasana</s>
made the Brahma missile, which wards off all missiles;
by it that Raudra missile, devourer of the world, was brought to rest.
When that missile had been repelled, <s>Viṣṇu</s>, destroyer of dānavas,
made the Kāladanda missile, terrifying to all the worlds.
As that was being set, a harsh wind blew,

children.text: cakampe ca mahī devī daityā bhinnadhiyo'bhavan ||
children.translated_text: the goddess Earth trembled, and the daityas became confused in mind.
Seeing that fierce missile, the dānavas, maddened by battle,
made divine missiles of many forms in the conflict.

children.text: nārāyaṇāstraṃ grasano gṛhītvā cakraṃ nimiḥ svāstravaraṃ mumoca
children.translated_text: <s>Grasana</s> took up the Nārāyaṇa missile, and <s>Nimi</s> released the discus, the best of his own weapons;
and <s>Jambha</s> made the Aiṣīka missile to ward off that Kāladanda missile.

children.text: yāvanna saṃdhyā na daśāṃ prayānti daityeśvarāścāstranivāraṇāya
children.translated_text: Before the lords of the daityas could reach the stage of countering the missile,
in that very instant it slew crores of daitya lords, together with elephants and horses.
Afterward that Kāladanda missile became pacified through the conjunction of the daitya missiles;

children.text: śāntaṃ tadālokya hariḥ svaśastraṃ svavikrame manyuparītamūrtiḥ ||
children.translated_text: seeing his own weapon pacified, <s>Hari</s>, his body filled with wrath in his valor,
took up the discus, shining like ten thousand suns, with a fierce rim, as if it were his own second self.
he hurled it, aiming at the commander, at his neck, fierce and diamond-hard.

children.text: cakraṃ tadākāśagataṃ vilokya sarvātmanā daityavarāḥ svavīryaiḥ
children.translated_text: Seeing that discus moving through the sky, all the foremost daityas, with all their strength and valor,

children.text: nāśaknuvanvārayituṃ pracaṇḍaṃ daivaṃ yathā karma mudhā prapannam ||
children.translated_text: were unable to check the fierce one, just as destiny, when karma has come upon one, is met in vain.

children.text: tamapratarkyaṃ janayannajayyaṃ cakraṃ papāta grasanasya kaṇṭhe
children.translated_text: That inconceivable, unconquerable, terror-producing discus fell upon <s>Grasana</s>'s neck,

children.text: dvidhā tu kṛtvā grasanasya kaṇṭhaṃ tadraktadhārāruṇaghoranābhi
children.translated_text: and, cutting <s>Grasana</s>'s neck in two, its terrible nave reddened by streams of his blood,
it went again to <s>Janārdana</s>'s hand, shining like a great blazing fire.
When that daitya <s>Grasana</s>, a lord among beings, had been slain,
the dānavas fought without restraint against <s>Hari</s>.
With paṭṭiśa spears, clubs, nooses, maces, and even corpses,
and with sharp-pointed nārāca arrows, discuses, and śakti lances,
<s>Janārdana</s>, the artful warrior, took the weapons released by the dānavas
and split each single one into hundreds with arrows like flames of fire.
Then, when the dānavas, their weapons and strength exhausted and their minds reeling,
became unable to take up weapons in the battle,
they fought <s>Janārdana</s> with dead elephants and horses;
the daityas, in tens of millions on every side, fought back from all directions.
Having made his form manifold, <s>Viṣṇu</s> became somewhat eased in his arms,
and in that exceedingly tumultuous battle he said to <s>Garutmat</s>,
"<s>Garutmat</s>, are you still untired even now in this battle?
If you are not tired, then go toward <s>Mathana</s>'s chariot.
But if you are tired, withdraw from the battle for a moment."
Thus addressed by that powerful <s>Viṣṇu</s>, <s>Garuḍa</s>
approached in battle the daitya <s>Mathana</s>, terrible to behold.
But the daitya, seeing before him the bearer of conch, discus, and mace,
struck him in the chest with a bhindipāla weapon and a sharpened arrow.
Without even heeding that blow, <s>Viṣṇu</s>, in that great battle,
struck him with five polished arrows, sharpened on stone,
and again struck him between the breasts with ten and with eight.
Pierced in his vital spots by <s>Hari</s>'s arrows, the lord of daityas trembled.

children.text: sa muhūrtaṃ samāśvāsya jagrāha parighaṃ tadā ||
children.translated_text: After recovering for a moment, he then seized an iron club,
and struck <s>Janārdana</s> too with that club, which had the brilliance of fire.
By that blow <s>Viṣṇu</s> was made to reel somewhat.
Then <s>Mādhava</s>, his eyes turned with anger, seized his mace,
and in fury crushed <s>Mathana</s> together with his chariot.
Then that daitya lord fell like a mountain at the time of destruction.
When that mighty dānava had fallen upon the ground,
the daityas sank into despair like elephants in mud.
Then, when those exceedingly proud dānavas were ruined,
<s>Mahiṣa</s>, lord of the dānavas, his eyes red with fury,
terrible and relying on the strength of his own arms, advanced against <s>Hari</s>.
<s>Mahiṣa</s> attacked <s>Hari</s> with a sharp-edged spear,
and the heroic <s>Mahiṣa</s> struck <s>Garuḍa</s> in the heart with a śakti lance.
Then, turning open his mouth, like the cave of a great mountain,
the daitya wished in battle to swallow <s>Garutmat</s> and <s>Acyuta</s>.
But <s>Acyuta</s>, perceiving the dānava's intention,
filled his mouth with divine missiles, the mighty one.
Then the one whose banner bears <s>Garuḍa</s> released a flood of arrows against <s>Mahiṣa</s>,
blocking his mouth with divine arrows consecrated by divine missiles.
Struck by those arrows, <s>Mahiṣa</s>, resembling a mountain,
his body overturned downward, fell, but he did not die.

children.text: mahiṣaṃ patitaṃ dṛṣṭvā bhūmau provāca keśavaḥ
children.translated_text: Seeing <s>Mahiṣa</s> fallen on the ground, <s>Keśava</s> said,
"Mad <s>Mahīṣāsura</s>, you do not deserve death here from me by weapons.
You were formerly declared by the lotus-born one himself to be killable by a woman.
Rise; preserve your life; go quickly away from this battle."
When that daitya <s>Mahiṣa</s> had turned away, the dānava <s>Śumbha</s>,
his lips clenched in anger and his face crooked with a frown,
rubbing hand against hand, took up a fearsome bow,
strung that bow, and took arrows resembling venomous serpents.

children.text: sa citrayodhī dṛḍhamuṣṭipātastatastu viṣṇuṃ garuḍaṃ ca daityaḥ
children.translated_text: Then that daitya, an artful warrior with a firm grip, attacked <s>Viṣṇu</s> and <s>Garuḍa</s>
with countless arrows hurled forth, resembling blazing tongues of fire and not beaten back.
And <s>Viṣṇu</s>, though struck by the arrows of the daitya lord, took up a bhuśuṇḍī club like Death,

children.text: tayā bhuśuṇḍyā ca pipeṣa meṣaṃ śumbhasya pattraṃ dharaṇīdharābham ||
children.translated_text: and with that bhuśuṇḍī he crushed <s>Śumbha</s>'s ram-mount, which was like a mountain.

children.text: tasmādavaplutya hatācca meṣād bhūbhau padātiḥ sa tu daityanāthaḥ
children.translated_text: Leaping down from that slain ram, that lord of daityas stood on the earth as a foot soldier.
Then <s>Hari</s> released volleys of arrows at him as he stood on the ground, blazing like the fire of time's end.

children.text: śaraistribhistasya bhujaṃ bibheda ṣaḍbhiśca śīrṣaṃ daśabhiśca ketum
children.translated_text: With three arrows he pierced his arm, with six his head, and with ten his banner.
<s>Viṣṇu</s>, drawing his bow back to the ends of his ears, his eyes rolled in wrath, pierced the daitya.

children.text: sa tena viddho vyathito babhūva daityeśvaro visrutaśoṇitaughaḥ
children.translated_text: Pierced by him, tormented, and streaming torrents of blood, the lord of daityas became distressed.
Then, when his firmness had somewhat faltered, the bearer of conch, lotus, and <s>Śārṅga</s> said to him,
"You are to be slain by a maiden; leave the battle, O <s>Śumbhāsura</s>. Within very few days

children.text: vadhaṃ na matto'rhasi ceha mūḍha vṛthaiva kiṃ yuddhasamutsuko'si ||
children.translated_text: you do not deserve death from me here, fool. Why are you vainly so eager for battle?"

children.text: jambho vaco viṣṇumukhānniśamya nimiśca niṣpeṣṭumiyeṣa viṣṇum
children.translated_text: Hearing <s>Jambha</s>'s words from <s>Viṣṇu</s>'s mouth, <s>Nimi</s> too wished to crush <s>Viṣṇu</s>.

children.text: gadāmathodyamya nimiḥ pracaṇḍāṃ jaghāna gāḍhāṃ garuḍaṃ śirastaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Then, raising a fierce, heavy mace, <s>Nimi</s> struck <s>Garuḍa</s> forcefully on the head.
<s>Śumbha</s> too struck <s>Viṣṇu</s> on the head with a parigha club, bright with varied gleams from masses of polished jewels.
Under the harsh blows from the two dānavas, the two fell to the earth, like a cloud and fire in splendor.

children.text: tatkarma dṛṣṭvā ditijāstu sarve jagarjuruccaiḥ kṛtasiṃhanādāḥ
children.translated_text: Seeing that deed, all the sons of <s>Diti</s> roared loudly, uttering lion-cries.
They twanged their bows, and with fierce blows against the gods they seemed to tear even the earth apart.

children.text: vāsāṃsi caivādudhuvuḥ pare tu dadhmuśca śaṅkhānakagomukhaughān ||
children.translated_text: Others waved their garments, and they blew hosts of conches, drums, and gomukha horns.
Then <s>Garuḍa</s>, together with <s>Keśava</s>, quickly regained consciousness.
Turning away from that battle, he fled with great speed.
<s>Sūta</s> said:
Seeing <s>Hari</s> fleeing, his banner and bow fallen away,

children.text: hariṃ devaḥ sahasrākṣo mene bhagnaṃ durāhave ||
children.translated_text: the thousand-eyed god thought that <s>Hari</s> had been broken in the terrible combat.
And seeing the daityas delighted, he could not discover what ought to be done.
Then the lord of gods, the chastiser of <s>Pāka</s>, came near to <s>Viṣṇu</s>.
He spoke to him sweetly, in words full of encouragement:
"Why are you playing with these evil-minded dānavas, O god?
When wicked men have found a person's vulnerable point, what action is then possible for him?
A low man, overlooked by one who is strong, imagines the strength to be his own.
Therefore a wise man should not disregard a low enemy simply because he is without a stronghold.
For chariot-warriors obtain victory through the success of those who go before them.
Who was your ally standing before you, O lord, when <s>Hiraṇyākṣa</s> was slain?
The daitya <s>Hiraṇyakaśipu</s>, mighty in valor and swollen with pride,
when he met you, O asura, experienced a terrible bewilderment of memory.
And earlier, those very powerful daitya lords who hated the gods
came to destruction when they reached you, like moths reaching a fire.

children.text: yuge yuge ca daityānāṃ tvamevāntakaro hare ||
children.translated_text: Age after age, O <s>Hari</s>, you alone are the destroyer of the daityas.
So too today, here, O <s>Viṣṇu</s>, become the refuge of the gods who are sinking down."
Thus addressed, <s>Viṣṇu</s>, the mighty-armed one, then expanded in power.
Endowed with supreme prosperity, the support of all beings and slayer of foes,
<s>Adhokṣaja</s> then spoke to the thousand-eyed one words suited to the moment:

children.text: daityendrāḥ svairvadhopāyaiḥ śakyā hantuṃ hi nānyataḥ
children.translated_text: "Daitya lords can indeed be killed by their own appointed means of death, and not otherwise.
The daitya <s>Tāraka</s>, difficult to conquer, can be killed only by a child seven days old.
One has obtained death at a woman's hand; for another, a maiden is the instrument of death.
But the dānava <s>Jambha</s>, fierce in valor, has obtained the condition of being killable.
Therefore, with divine heroic power, strike down <s>Jambha</s>, foremost in the world.

children.text: avadhyaḥ sarvabhūtānāṃ tvāṃ vinā sa tu dānavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: That dānava is invulnerable to all beings except you.
Guarded by me in battle, uproot <s>Jambha</s>, the thorn of the world."
Hearing that speech of <s>Vaikuṇṭha</s>, the thousand-eyed slayer of the enemies of the immortals
commanded all the gods concerning the arrangement of the army.
Whatever essence of valor and of tapas there was in all the worlds,
that <s>Hari</s> made the eleven <s>Rudras</s> leaders in the van.
Powerful, blue-throated, and girded with coils of serpents around their bodies,
adorned with lofty crests bearing crescent moons and garlands of human skulls,
their bodies smeared with the flames of tridents, terrifying with the circles of their arms,
with tawny, high-piled masses of matted hair, and wearing lion skins,
the <s>Rudras</s>, beginning with <s>Kapālīśa</s>, routed the great asuras.
<s>Kapālī</s>, <s>Piṅgala</s>, <s>Bhīma</s>, <s>Virūpākṣa</s>, <s>Vilohita</s>,
<s>Ajeśa</s>, <s>Śāsana</s>, <s>Śāstā</s>, <s>Śambhu</s>, <s>Caṇḍa</s>, and also <s>Dhruva</s>:
these were the eleven powerful <s>Rudras</s> of endless strength.
Guarding the front of the army and tearing apart the dānavas,
they refreshed the Thirty gods, roaring like clouds.
On great <s>Airāvata</s>, like the <s>Himālaya</s> and garlanded with golden lotuses,
adorned with waving chowries and clusters of golden bells,
the four-tusked elephant, vast as a mountain,
streaming great ichor and able to assume any form, <s>Śatakratu</s>
stood shining on him like the radiant sun on the peak of <s>Himagiri</s>.
The wind-god, of immeasurable valor, guarded his left side.
Fire guarded the other, filling the quarters with flame.
<s>Viṣṇu</s> became the rear-guard of <s>Śatakratu</s> together with his army.
The <s>Ādityas</s>, the <s>Vasus</s>, the <s>Viśve Devas</s>, the <s>Maruts</s>, and the two <s>Aśvins</s>,
with gandharvas, rākṣasas, yakṣas, kinnaras, and great serpents,
bearing many kinds of bright weapons and adorned with golden ornaments,
formed marked divisions in crores upon crores.
Letting their own fame resound, with companies of bards going before them,
the races of gods, together with <s>Indra</s>, moved joyfully to slay the daityas.
That bannered army of <s>Śatakratu</s>, protected by hosts of immortals and resounding with hundreds of elephants and horses,
adorned with crores of white, lofty flags and streamers, became an increaser of sorrow for the sons of <s>Diti</s>.
Then, seeing the army of the gods approaching, <s>Gajāsura</s>
in elephant form appeared terrible, like a mass of great rain clouds.
The daitya, armed with a battle-axe and with his lips pressed tight around his tusks,
crushed the gods in battle and hurled others away with his trunk.
He struck others with his axe, that lord of daityas of furious valor.
As he was felling the army, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras
all together released a mass of various missiles and weapons.
They hurled nooses, battle-axes, discus-weapons, bhindipālas, and heavy clubs.
lances, darts, sharp swords, and unbearable mallets,
that fierce daitya swallowed all of them, as a herd-leader would swallow morsels.
Striking them down with the crack of his long trunk, lashed about in anger,
the elephant-dānava moved through the battle among the gods, terrible to behold.
In whatever host of gods <s>Gajāsura</s> fell upon,
in each one there arose a great noise, made of cries of panic.
Then, seeing that army fleeing on every side,
the Rudras, whose flames had arisen from proud wrath, said to one another:

children.text: bho bho gṛhṇīta daityendraṃ mardatainaṃ hatāśrayam
children.translated_text: "Ho! ho! Seize the lord of daityas; crush this one whose support is gone.
Drag him with sharp tridents, and break him in his vital parts."
Hearing the words, <s>Kapālī</s> took up his trident with its sharp-pointed tip;
wiping it with his left hand, his eyes opened wide in fury,
he rushed in battle toward the lord of daityas, his brow bent in a frown,
holding the spotless trident fast in a firm clenched fist.
<s>Kapālī</s> struck the elephant-dānava on the temple,

children.text: tato daśāpi te rudrā nirmalāyomayai raṇe ||
children.translated_text: and then all ten of those Rudras, in battle, with spotless iron tridents,
struck the lord of daityas, whose body was like a mountain, in the fight.
With openings from which blood streamed, tormented by the tips of sharp tridents,
the dark-hued daitya shone like a clear lake in autumn,
crowded on every side with masses of fully blossomed red and blue lotuses,
and surrounded, as if by swans, by the Rudras whose bodies were white with ash.
Then the daitya, with distress approaching and his ear-flaps shaking,
<s>Gajāsura</s> pierced <s>Śambhu</s> in the region of the navel with his tusks.

children.text: dṛṣṭvā saktaṃ tu rudrābhyāṃ nava rudrāstato'dbhutam ||
children.translated_text: Seeing him engaged with the two Rudras, the nine Rudras then, in a wondrous way,
cut the body of the enemy of the immortals with various weapons.
Fearless and strong, they stood firm in battle on the battlefield,
like jackals in the forest when they have found a dead buffalo.
Leaving <s>Kapālin</s>, the foremost asura went off,
and, angered, the daitya swiftly attacked the nine Rudras.
He crushed them with blows of his feet, and also with his tusks and trunk.
When, through that tumultuous battle with them, he had come to exhaustion,
then <s>Kapālī</s> seized the trunk of that enemy of the immortals.
He whirled <s>Gajāsura</s> with great speed and extreme force.
Seeing the daitya worn out by fatigue, with only a little life still quivering,
spiritless in that battle, his eager delight in fighting gone,

children.text: tataḥ patata evāsya carma cotkṛtya bhairavam ||
children.translated_text: then, even as he was falling, <s>Kapālī</s> cut off his fearsome hide,
streaming floods of blood from every limb, and made it his own garment.
Seeing the daitya slain, the dānava lords, though very powerful,
were terrified; by the thousands they fled, ran off, departed, and fell.
Seeing the form of <s>Kapālin</s> covered with an elephant-hide garment,

children.text: dikṣu bhūmau tamevograṃ rudraṃ daityā vyalokayan
children.translated_text: the daityas saw that same fierce <s>Rudra</s> in the quarters and upon the earth.
When that mighty lord of dānavas had thus been shattered,
then the daitya lord, mounted on an elephant, after the war-drum had been beaten,
with a dānava force hard to withstand and resembling clouds at the end of the kalpa,
<s>Nimi</s> rushed swiftly forward, trampling the armies of the gods.

children.text: yāṃ yāṃ nimigajo yāti diśaṃ tāṃ tāṃ savāhanā
children.translated_text: Whatever direction <s>Nimi</s>'s elephant went,
the gods, with their mounts, abandoned that direction and fled in fear, casting away their weapons.
The elephants of the gods fled from the scent of that elephant.
When the armies of the gods had fled, <s>Pākaśāsana</s>
stood together with the eight guardians of the quarters and with <s>Keśava</s>.
As soon as <s>Nimi</s>'s elephant came up against <s>Śakra</s>'s elephant,

children.text: tāvacchakragajo yāto muktvā nādaṃ sa bhairavam ||
children.translated_text: <s>Śakra</s>'s elephant departed, letting out a terrible cry.

children.text: dhriyamāṇo'pi yatnena sa raṇe naiva tiṣṭhati
children.translated_text: Though restrained with effort, it would not stand at all in the battle.
When that elephant fled, <s>Pākaśāsana</s>, mounted upon it,
fought facing backward against the army of the lord of dānavas.
But <s>Śatakratu</s> struck <s>Nimi</s> on the chest with his thunderbolt,
and with his mace he struck that elephant firmly on the cheek.
Taking no thought of that blow, <s>Nimi</s>, possessed of fearless valor,
struck <s>Airāvaṇa</s> in the waist with a mallet.
Then, struck by the mallet in the fight, <s>Śakra</s>'s elephant
went backward on its feet over the earth, mountain-like in form.
Quickly rising through its agility, the great elephant of the immortals
swiftly withdrew from the battle, terrified by <s>Nimi</s>'s elephant.
Then a harsh wind blew, full of much gravel and dust.
Facing him, <s>Nimi</s>'s elephant shook mountains with its speed.
With blood streaming, it shone like a mountain with lakes of dense mineral color.
<s>Dhaneśa</s> also hurled a heavy mace at that dānava elephant.
Thrown with force, it fell upon the head of that lord of daityas' elephant.
That elephant, stunned by the fall of the mace,
split the earth swiftly with its tusks and fell like a mountain.
When that elephant had fallen, there arose a great lion-roar
on every side from the armies of the gods, with the trumpeting of elephants,
with the neighing cry of horses, and with the twanging of bowstrings by bowmen.

children.text: gajaṃ taṃ nihataṃ dṛṣṭvā nimiṃ cāpi parāṅmukham ||
children.translated_text: Seeing that elephant slain and <s>Nimi</s> also turned away,
and hearing the lion-roar of the gods, the very wrathful <s>Jambha</s>

children.text: jambho jajvāla kopena pītājya iva pāvakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: blazed with anger like fire fed with drunk ghee.
Red-eyed with anger, he set an arrow upon his bow against the gods,
and saying, "Stand!" he at once urged on his charioteer.
As that chariot moved swiftly, its brilliance became
like that of a thousand suns risen on the mountain of sunrise.
In battle, with that chariot bearing banners and wreathed with networks of little bells,
and with a moon-white parasol, by that very car
he was seen striking terror into the hearts of the gods' armies.
Seeing him coming, with an arrow set upon his bow,
<s>Śatakratu</s>, his spirit undaunted, drew his bow firmly.
He took an arrow with an oil-polished point, crescent-headed and straight.

children.text: tenāsya saśaraṃ cāpaṃ raṇe cicheda vṛtrahā
children.translated_text: With that, in battle, <s>Vṛtrahā</s> cut his bow together with its arrow.
Quickly abandoning that bow, <s>Jambha</s>, delight of the dānavas,
took up another bow, swift and able to bear a heavy draw,
and arrows shaped like venomous serpents, oil-polished and straight.
He pierced <s>Śakra</s> in the region of the collarbone with ten feathered arrows,

children.text: hṛdaye ca tribhiścāpi dvābhyāṃ ca skandhayor dvayoḥ ||
children.translated_text: and also in the heart with three, and in both shoulders with two.
<s>Śakra</s> too sent against the lord of dānavas just such a net of arrows.
But before the arrows shot by <s>Śakra</s>'s arms had reached him, the lord of dānavas
cut them in ten in the sky with arrows like flames of fire.
Then, with a net of arrows, <s>Devendra</s> carefully covered the lord of dānavas,
as in the rainy season the clouds cover the sky.
The daitya too scattered that net of arrows with sharp shafts,
as the wind scatters a dense mass of clouds after enclosing the faces of the quarters.
Then, when <s>Śakra</s>, in the agitation of anger, could not gain an advantage
over the lord of dānavas, he made the Gandharva weapon, exceedingly wondrous.
The path of movement became pervaded by the radiance that arose from it,
and by cities of the gandharvas, with various ramparts and gateways,
which, of wonderful form, released showers of missiles on every side.
Then, struck by that shower of missiles, the great army of the daityas
came for refuge to <s>Jambha</s>, whose valor was immeasurable.
Though the daitya himself was bewildered, oppressed by the weapon of <s>Sahasrākṣa</s>,
remembering the conduct of the virtuous, he became intent on protecting the frightened.
Then the son of <s>Diti</s> released the weapon called Mausala.
Thereupon the whole world became filled with iron clubs,
irresistible on every side and able to strike with a single blow.
Among them was the Gandharva city fashioned by the Gandharva weapon.
Having set another Gandharva weapon against the armies of the gods,
with each single blow he struck elephants, horses, great chariot-warriors,
chariots and horses; he quickly slew them by hundreds and by thousands.
Then the lord of the gods sent forth the Tvāṣṭra weapon.
As the Tvāṣṭra weapon was being aimed, flames of fire issued forth.
Then divine mechanical weapons, hard to withstand, came forth.
By those machines a canopy was formed in the sky.
When, by that canopy, the Mausala weapon had gone to rest,
<s>Jambha</s> released the mountain weapon, which battered the mass of machines.
Then there came a rain of stones, each a fathom in size.
Immediately afterward, the machines produced by the Tvāṣṭra weapon
were reduced to fragments like sesame seeds by that fall of stones.
Having reduced the machines to bits, the mountain weapon, upon the heads of the enemy,
fell with extreme speed and then tore open the earth.
Then the thousand-eyed <s>Puraṃdara</s> made the Vajra weapon.
At that, the great rain of stones was shattered on every side.
Then, when the mountain weapon had been pacified, <s>Jambha</s>, like a mountain,
fearless and of exceeding valor, made the Aiṣīka weapon.
By the Aiṣīka weapon, the Vajra weapon dear to <s>Śakra</s> came to destruction.
And as that Aiṣīka, a supreme and very hard-to-withstand weapon, expanded,
the armies of the gods, with their chariots and elephants, blazed up.
As the battle-lines were being burned by its heat, the best of the gods,
the powerful <s>Pākaśāsana</s>, made the Āgneya weapon.
By that weapon, that other weapon then collapsed.
When that weapon had been checked, the fire weapon blazed forth.

children.text: jajvāla kāyaṃ jambhasya sarathaṃ ca sasārathim ||
children.translated_text: It set <s>Jambha</s>'s body ablaze, together with his chariot and charioteer.
Then that lord of daityas, checked but quick-witted,
released the Vāruṇa weapon, the pacifier of the flames of fire.
Then the sky, crowded with clouds filled with flashing creepers of lightning,
seemed filled with the deep sound of mṛdaṅga drums.
With streams of water like the trunks of lordly elephants
falling from the sky, the whole world appeared filled in an instant.
Seeing that the Āgneya weapon had been quieted, the lord of the gods
made the Vāyavya weapon, destroyer of the mass of clouds.
Then, by the power of the Vāyavya weapon, when the circle of clouds had been driven away,
the sky became clear, with the radiance of a blue-lotus petal.
And those dānavas, shaken by the exceedingly terrible wind,

children.text: na śekustatra te sthātuṃ raṇe 'tibalino'pi ye ||
children.translated_text: could not stand there in battle, even though they were very strong.
Then <s>Jambha</s> became a mountain ten yojanas broad,
to ward off the wind and to remove the fear of the dānavas.
Its trees blazed with the lofty splendor of many released weapons.
Then, when the wind had been quieted and the lord of daityas had taken mountain form,
<s>Śatakratu</s> quickly released a great thunderbolt, made of vajra.
When that thunderbolt fell upon the daitya who had the form of an immovable mountain,
The caves split apart, and waterfalls collapsed all around.
Then that mountain-magic of the lord of <s>dānavas</s> came to an end.
When his mountain-magic had ceased, the lord of <s>dānavas</s>, swollen with pride,
became a terrible elephant, equal in shape to a great mountain.
He crushed the army of the gods, and with his tusks he struck the gods as well.
The <s>dānava</s> broke some from behind, wrapping them around with his trunk.
Then, as he was destroying the armies of the gods, <s>Vṛtrahā</s>
released the <s>Nārasiṃha</s> astra, irresistible in the three worlds.
Then thousands of lions came forth through the power of the mantra,
with black fangs, roaring laughter, and claws like saws.
His body was torn open by them, and he cast off his elephant-magic.
Then he became a terrible venomous serpent, crowded with a hundred hoods.
When the army of the gods had been burned by his poisonous breath, that great chariot-warrior
<s>Śakra</s>, fair-armed, then employed the <s>Gāruḍa</s> astra.
Then thousands of <s>Garutmats</s> came forth from that astra.
Assailed by those <s>Garutmats</s>, <s>Jambha</s>, who had taken the form of a serpent,

children.text: kṛtastu khaṇḍaśo daityaḥ sāsya māyā vyanaśyata
children.translated_text: was cut into pieces, and that magic of the <s>daitya</s> vanished.

children.text: pranaṣṭāyāṃ tu māyāyāṃ tato jambho mahāsuraḥ
children.translated_text: But when the magic had vanished, then <s>Jambha</s>, the great <s>asura</s>,
made an incomparable form that reached the path of the moon and sun.
With his mouth gaping wide, he wished to swallow the foremost gods.
Then great chariot-warriors with elephants entered his mouth,
terrible as the army of the gods entered it, with its palate stretched open to <s>Pātāla</s>.
As the armies were being swallowed by the very powerful <s>dānava</s>,
<s>Śakra</s>, his arms exhausted and his mount with him, fell into despair.
He could not understand what should be done, and he said this to <s>Janārdana</s>:
"What further action remains to be done here?
Relying on what means should we, eager for battle, strive against this <s>dānava</s>?"
Then <s>Hari</s>, noble-minded, said this to the wielder of the thunderbolt:
"The battle must not now be abandoned by you, O terror of the timid.
Quickly increase your great magical power against the foe, O <s>Puraṃdara</s>.
I have marked this <s>daitya</s>; he has been mastered by me, though he has gained his valor.

children.text: mā śakra mohamāgaccha kṣipramastraṃ smara prabho ||
children.translated_text: Do not fall into confusion, O <s>Śakra</s>; quickly remember the astra, my lord."

children.text: tataḥ śakraḥ prakupito dānavaṃ prati devarāṭ
children.translated_text: Then <s>Śakra</s>, king of the gods, enraged against the <s>dānava</s>,
carefully released the <s>Nārāyaṇa</s> astra against the <s>asura</s>'s chest.
Meanwhile the <s>daitya</s>, his mouth gaping open, swallowed in an instant
three lakhs of gandharvas, kiṃnaras, serpents, and rākṣasas.
Then that <s>Nārāyaṇa</s> astra fell upon the <s>asura</s>'s chest.
His heart split by the great astra, he streamed with blood.
The son of the <s>asuras</s> gave forth a vomit like a battlefield enclosure.
By the fiery power of that astra, the <s>daitya</s>'s form was destroyed.
Then the <s>daitya</s> disappeared, unseen in the sky.
Standing in the sky, that lord of <s>daityas</s>, beyond the reach of the senses,
released weapons as the supreme cause for the destruction of the armies of the gods.
Spears, axes, discus-weapons, arrows, thunderbolts, and heavy clubs,
hatchets together with swords, bhindipālas, and iron balls,
the fierce <s>dānava</s> rained down, unfailing and inexhaustible.
By those terrifying weapons released by the <s>dānava</s> upon the armies of the gods,
the earth was filled with arms and with heads still wearing earrings,
with thighs like elephant-trunks, and with lordly elephants like mountains,
and with chariots, along with their charioteers, whose poles, wheels, and axles were broken.
The earth became hard to traverse, muddy with flesh and blood,
with eddies and pools from torrents of blood, and with heaps of corpses like rocky mounds.
It was crowded with dancing headless trunks, a mire of flowing fat and blood, like the destruction of the three worlds alike for all embodied beings.

children.text: śṛgālagṛdhravāyasāḥ paraṃ pramodamādadhuḥ kvacidvikṛṣṭalocanaḥ śavasya rauti vāyasaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Jackals, vultures, and crows took the highest delight; somewhere a crow cried out while pulling an eye from a corpse.

children.text: vikṛṣṭapīvarāntrakāḥ prayānti jambukāḥ kvacit kvacitsthito'tibhīṣaṇaḥ śvacañcucarvito bakaḥ
children.translated_text: Somewhere jackals went along dragging plump entrails; somewhere a very dreadful crane stood, chewing what dogs and beaks had torn.

children.text: mṛtasya māṃsamāharañchvajātayaśca saṃsthitāḥ kvacidvṛko gajāsṛjaṃ papau nilīyatāntrataḥ ||
children.translated_text: Dog-packs stood there carrying off the flesh of the dead; somewhere a wolf drank elephant-blood while hidden among entrails.

children.text: kvacit turaṃgamaṇḍalī vikṛṣyate śvajātibhiḥ kvacitpiśācajātakaiḥ prapītaśoṇitāsavaiḥ
children.translated_text: Somewhere a herd of horses was dragged about by packs of dogs; somewhere by bands of piśācas who had drunk the liquor of blood,

children.text: svakāminīyutairdrutaṃ pramodamattasaṃbhramair mamaitadānayānanaṃ khuro'yamastu me priyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: together with their beloved women, hurrying in joy, intoxication, and excitement: "Bring me that face; let this hoof be mine, dear!"

children.text: karo'yamabjasaṃnibho mamāstu karṇapūrakaḥ saroṣam īkṣate'parā vapāṃ vinā priyaṃ tadā
children.translated_text: "Let this lotus-like hand be my ear-ornament." Then another woman angrily looked at her beloved, who had no omentum.

children.text: parā priyā hyavāpa yadbhṛtoṣṇaśoṇitāsavaṃ vikṛṣya śavacarma tatprabaddhasāndrapallavam ||
children.translated_text: Another beloved woman obtained a liquor of fresh hot blood; dragging away that corpse-skin, with its thick flaps attached,

children.text: cakāra yakṣakāminī taruṃ kuṭhārapāṭitaṃ gajasya dantamātmajaṃ pragṛhya kumbhasaṃpuṭam
